author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Bone-conduction headphones can keep a listener aware of traffic and other surroundings, but they do not remove the risk of hearing damage, according to a new NHPR Outside/In explainer. The devices transmit vibrations through the skull to the cochlea instead of sending sound through the outer ear.

That open-ear design can be useful for runners, cyclists and others who need to hear what is happening nearby. The tradeoff is that loud playback still reaches the same sensitive structures in the inner ear. Prolonged exposure at high volume can therefore cause the same kind of damage associated with conventional headphones.

University of Michigan noise-exposure researcher Rick Neitzel told the program that weak bass and background noise can lead users to raise the volume. In a loud setting, noise-canceling headphones may allow comfortable listening at a lower level because they reduce the competing sound rather than trying to overpower it.

Practical safeguards remain familiar: use phone volume limits and monitoring tools, take listening breaks, and move to a quieter place when possible. Bone-conduction models may offer an awareness advantage outdoors, but the safer choice still depends on volume, duration and the surrounding noise—not simply on how audio reaches the ear.
dek: The open-ear devices may improve awareness outdoors, but specialists say excessive volume still reaches and can injure the inner ear.
headline: NHPR explainer warns bone-conduction headphones can still damage hearing
